name: Critiques and null findings on AI and entry-level employment

Stanford Digital Economy Lab, News / Insights, 9 February 2026. https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/news/canaries-interest-rates-and-timinga-more-on-recent-drivers-of-employment-changes-for-young-workers

D2: think-tank in-house analysis, not peer-reviewed. None of the eight documents is peer-reviewed.

author_credentials: A: Erik Brynjolfsson (Stanford HAI professor, Director of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, NBER research associate), Bharat Chandar (labor economist, Research Director at the Lab), Ruyu Chen (research scientist at the Lab). They are the authors of the paper being criticised, so this is a reply, not an independent check. B: Anders Humlum (economist, University of Chicago Booth, NBER) and Emilie Vestergaard (economist, University of Copenhagen). Funding stated as Booth's Center for Applied Artificial Intelligence and the Polsky Center; no AI vendor interest stated. C: Martha Gimbel (Executive Director, Budget Lab at Yale), Molly Kinder (Senior Fellow, Brookings Metro), Joshua Kendall (Research Fellow), Maddie Lee (Research Assistant); C2 adds Ryan Nunn. No commercial interest stated. D1: Zanna Iscenko is 'AI & Economy Lead, Chief Economist's Team, Google' and Fabien Curto Millet is 'Chief Economist, Google'. This is a commercial interest: Google sells generative AI, and the essay argues AI is not the cause of entry-level job losses. Acknowledgements thank Google executives (Ruth Porat, Kent Walker, James Manyika) alongside academics. exact_quotes: A (opening summary): 'While interest rates affect overall employment, existing evidence does not suggest they are a good explanation for the disproportionate decline in entry-level hiring in AI-exposed occupations.'

A (opening summary): 'On the timing, we do find suggestive evidence that when you include the broadest set of controls (firm-time fixed-effects), the timing of the employment decline in AI-exposed occupations becomes significant only in 2024; the earlier declines are likely (at least partly) due to some combination of other factors, not just AI.'

A (section 'The Timing of Employment Declines in AI-Exposed Occupations'): 'While these charts are suggestive of a relationship between AI and employment, we can't be sure of the causality from this sort of analysis.'

A (same section): 'we do not believe that AI is always and everywhere the sole determinant of employment, and we do not encourage others to interpret our results in that way. For example, the precipitous decline in employment for young software developers is a consequence of various factors. Even if employment outcomes diverge notably only after the release of ChatGPT, this could be driven by other changes that occurred at the same time.'

A (Conclusion): 'With the fixed-effect approach, the employment changes start later, but they are growing (reaching about 16% by October 2025, vs 13% in our paper with data only through July), and they have not shown a reversal.'
A (Conclusion): 'Since we don't have an experiment where we can compare a world with AI to one without, this will remain an active area for scientific research and discussion.'

B1 (abstract, May 2025): 'we estimate precise zeros: AI chatbots have had no significant impact on earnings or recorded hours in any occupation, with confidence intervals ruling out effects larger than 1%. Modest productivity gains (average time savings of 3%), combined with weak wage pass-through, help explain these limited labor market effects. Our findings challenge narratives of imminent labor market transformation due to Generative AI.'

B2 (abstract, revised March 2026): 'using difference-indifferences, we estimate precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours at both the worker and workplace levels, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after the launch of ChatGPT.' [sic: 'difference-indifferences' as printed]
B2 (abstract): 'Technological change reshapes work well before it surfaces in earnings or hours.'

B2 (introduction, p.4): 'While we replicate the pattern of declining early-career employment in exposed occupations in Denmark, our difference-in-differences analysis reveals that the declines are not driven by firms adopting AI chatbots.'

B2 (section 3.4 'Workplace Employment', p.30): 'Difference-in-differences estimates show no differential changes in the employment share of early-career workers at adopting workplaces, with estimates precise enough to rule out effects greater than a third of a percentage point.'

B2 (section 3.4, pp.31-32): 'This suggests that other forces, such as changes in the macroeconomic environment or anticipatory hiring freezes unrelated to actual adoption, may be driving the aggregate pattern.'

B2 (conclusion): 'the absence of measurable labor market effects is not evidence that nothing is happening—but rather that transformation is occurring on margins that conventional economic statistics do not capture.'

C1 (introduction): 'Overall, our metrics indicate that the broader labor market has not experienced a discernible disruption since ChatGPT's release 33 months ago, undercutting fears that AI automation is currently eroding the demand for cognitive labor across the economy.'

C1 (section 'Recent College Graduates'): 'The dissimilarity has increased slightly faster in recent months than it did in a previous time period, which could be consistent with a recent paper from Brynjolfsson et al. showing a possible impact of AI on employment of early career workers. It could also simply reflect a slowing labor market. However, our results should be interpreted with caution particularly given small sample sizes.'
C1 (Key Takeaways): 'Currently, measures of exposure, automation, and augmentation show no sign of being related to changes in employment or unemployment.'
C2 (Key Takeaways): 'So far, this approach provides no clear evidence of AI effects on the labor market, but this could change quickly'

C2 (body): 'the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Current Population Survey, our data source throughout this analysis, is best suited to analysis of broad groups and somewhat underpowered for subgroup analysis, like the 22–27 year old recent college graduates that have been a special focus in some AI labor market impact discussions. If labor market effects of AI are currently limited to a narrow slice of the workforce, other datasets and research designs would be better suited to identify them.'

D1 (p.1): 'The most plausible explanation is that the data patterns observed are not early warnings of large-scale technological displacement, but rather the predictable consequences of a classic macroeconomic shock: the sharpest monetary policy tightening cycle in four decades.'
D1 (p.2, 'The Trouble with Timing'): 'The central weakness of the hypothesis that AI is the main driver of the recent entry-level downturn is its implausible timeline.'

D1 (p.3): 'vacancies for the highest AI exposure quintile of occupations peaked in March–April 2022 and declined sharply throughout the remainder of the year. This hiring slowdown predates any plausible generative AI effect by over six months.'
D1 (p.3): 'There is no evidence that job postings for junior roles within occupations most exposed to AI have declined more than postings for senior positions.'
D1 (p.8): 'absence of evidence is not the same as evidence of absence'

D1 (p.8): 'it will be necessary to profoundly rethink education for the new world of work as well as on-the-job training (especially should AI take over tasks which were previously seen as formative).'
D2 (section on young workers): 'Unemployment rates have been creeping up for young workers and recent graduates alike, whether they are AI-exposed or not.'
D2: 'The lack of causal evidence is a problem, in fact, not just for all of our analyses presented here but also for any investigation that uses the available measures of AI exposure.'
key_claims: A (Stanford authors' reply). Two claims. (1) Interest rates are not a good explanation for the disproportionate decline: using Zens et al. (2020) estimates, more AI-exposed occupations are on average less interest-rate sensitive, and the most AI-exposed occupations show larger early-career declines within both the below-median and above-median interest-rate-exposure groups. (2) A concession on timing: with firm-time fixed effects, the relative decline for the most-exposed 22 to 25 year olds 'starts becoming notable in 2024 (not late 2022 or 2023)', so the earlier part of the raw decline is at least partly due to other factors. They restate that the result is not causal and that AI is not the sole determinant, naming young software developers as a case with 'various factors'.

B (Humlum and Vestergaard, Denmark). Among 11 AI-exposed occupations, including software developers, chatbot adoption is widespread but has produced no detectable change in earnings or recorded hours for workers or workplaces. The revised paper adds a direct test of the Canaries pattern: Denmark shows the same aggregate fall in early-career (age 22 to 25) employment in exposed occupations, but workplaces that encourage chatbot use show no different change in their early-career employment share from those that do not. Their reading is that firms' actual adoption is not what is driving the fall. What does change is task content and occupational mobility.

C (Yale Budget Lab). C1: the economy-wide occupational mix has not shifted faster since ChatGPT than in earlier technology transitions in a way that can be attributed to AI, and the share of workers in high-exposure occupations is stable. On young graduates it reports a slight recent rise in dissimilarity that 'could be consistent with' Canaries or with a slowing labour market. C2 (May 2026): a synthetic difference-in-differences comparison of exposed and unexposed occupations finds 'no statistically or economically significant effects as of yet' on employment share or wages. It explicitly says CPS data are underpowered for the narrow early-career group.

D1 (Iscenko and Curto Millet, Google, published by EIG). The Canaries pattern is better explained by the 2022 monetary tightening than by AI. Job postings in the most AI-exposed quintile peaked in March to April 2022, before ChatGPT; a hiring freeze mechanically shrinks a narrow 22 to 25 age band because that band is restocked only by new hires; AI exposure and interest-rate sensitivity are correlated through sector mix; junior and senior postings fell roughly in parallel.

D2 (Eckhardt and Goldschlag, EIG). Across CPS-based measures (unemployment, labour-force exit, occupation switching, industry employment) and five AI-exposure measures, no meaningful AI effect is visible. Unemployment rose more for the least exposed workers than the most exposed, and unemployment has risen for young workers and recent graduates whether AI-exposed or not.

How these qualify the Canaries result, taken together: nobody disputes that early-career employment in AI-exposed occupations has fallen (Humlum and Vestergaard replicate it in Denmark). The dispute is attribution. The Stanford authors themselves now date the part that survives firm-level controls to 2024 onward and say the earlier decline is partly other factors; critics offer interest rates, pre-existing trends and remote work; and none of the null studies has the power or the data to rule out an effect confined to 22 to 25 year olds in the US.
headline_figures: A: 'reaching about 16% by October 2025, vs 13% in our paper with data only through July'. Unit: relative employment decline for the most AI-exposed workers aged 22 to 25, firm-time fixed-effect specification. Comparison group: less exposed occupations within the same firm and month. The note does not give a separate number for software developers.

A: timing. Decline in the fixed-effects event study 'starts becoming notable in 2024 (not late 2022 or 2023)'; elsewhere 'significant only in 2024' and 'significant only after 2024'. The wording differs between sentences of the same note.

B1 (May 2025): confidence intervals 'ruling out effects larger than 1%' on earnings and recorded hours (pooled difference-in-differences); dynamic estimates 'rule out changes larger than 2%'; occupation-level estimates 'generally excluding changes greater than 6%'. Outcomes tracked 'through June 2024—one and a half years after ChatGPT's launch'.
B1: 'users report average time savings of 2.8% of work hours' (abstract rounds to 3%); 'only 3–7% of workers' productivity gains are passed through to higher earnings'.

B1: sample 'about 25,000 workers from 7,000 workplaces across 11 occupations'; '115,000 workers' invited per survey round; employers: '38% deploy in-house models, and 30% of employees have received training'; encouragement lifts take-up 'from 47% to 83%'; 'AI chatbots have created new job tasks for 8.4% of workers'.
B2 (revised March 2026): 'ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after the launch of ChatGPT'; outcomes tracked 'through December 2024'.

B2: early-career share. Estimates 'rule out effects greater than a third of a percentage point' on the employment share of workers aged 22 to 25 at workplaces that encourage chatbot use, against a 'baseline share of about 8%' and an 'aggregate decline of about 0.6 percentage points between October 2022 and December 2024'. Footnote 21: adoption could account for 'at most a 0.43 × 0.33 ≈ 0.14 percentage point decline'. 'About 43% of workplaces encourage chatbot use.'

B2 (section 3.5 'Perceived Impacts'): 'Virtually all respondents—97.7% of adopters and 99.5% of non-adopters—state that AI chatbots have had no impact on their labor earnings.' Self-reported, late 2024 survey.
C1: 'the broader labor market has not experienced a discernible disruption since ChatGPT's release 33 months ago' (November 2022 to July 2025 CPS).

C1: occupational mix 'on a path only about 1 percentage point higher than it was at the turn of the 21st century with the adoption of the internet'; by 2002 the mix was 'at most around 7 percentage points different than it was in 1996'.

C1: recent graduates (ages 20-24) versus older graduates (25-34): dissimilarity 'rarely deviates outside of the 30-33% range' since January 2021. Sample: 'around 1,100 and 5,600 observations (3% and 12% of the overall sample), respectively' per year.

C1: share of workers in lowest, middle and highest exposure groups 'stable at around 29%, 46% and 18%, respectively'; unemployed workers were in occupations where 'about 25 to 35 percent of tasks, on average, could be performed by generative AI', with no upward trend.

C2: unemployment-rate appendix shows 'roughly half a percentage point increase in the entire sample, and more for the 16-34 year old subsample—but both are statistically insignificant as of the first quarter of 2026'. Employment: 'the top of the 95% confidence interval for the latest quarter is equivalent to only about 5% of that average share, and the point estimate itself in that quarter is virtually zero'.

D1: cites Canaries as 'a 16 percent relative decline in employment for early-career workers (ages 22–25) in the most AI-exposed occupations since the widespread release of generative AI in November 2022', while footnote 1 says the comments 'were written about the original version of the "Canaries" paper published on 26 August 2025' (the 13% vintage).
D1: 'By June 2023, almost a half of the total observed employment decline for ... software engineers and customer service workers, had already materialized.'

D1: hiring-freeze thought experiment: after a one-year freeze with zero layoffs, 'entry-level employment for the 22–25 year-old workers has shrunk by a shocking 25 percent while it remained level for all other age groups'.

D1: 'Approximately 38 percent of workers in the most AI-exposed quintile are employed in these sectors [Information, Finance and Insurance, Professional and Technical Services], compared to less than 2 percent in the least-exposed quintile.'

D1: Census BTOS: 'even in Q4 2023, fewer than 10 percent of large businesses surveyed were even planning to use AI in the next six months'; 'for Q3 2025 ... adoption by large businesses has only climbed to 12 percent'.

D1: 'unemployment rates of 4.8 percent for recent college graduates (aged 22–27) and 7.4 percent for all young workers in the same age group' (New York Fed); LinkedIn July 2025: 'entry-level hiring rates have declined 23 percent compared to pre-pandemic levels, a steeper drop than the 18 percent decline for overall hiring'.
D1: data: 'more than 238 million US job postings (averaging ~3.3 million monthly) from September 2019 to August 2025' (Lightcast).

D2: 'between 2022 and the beginning of 2025 the unemployment rate for the quintile of the most exposed workers rose by 0.30 percentage points. For the quintile of the least exposed workers, it climbed by 0.94 percentage points.'

D2: two LLM-based exposure measures show the most-exposed group's unemployment rising 'about a 0.2 percentage point' (Eloundou et al.) and 'about a 0.3 percentage point' (Eisfeldt et al.) relative to less exposed workers between 2022-2023 and 2024-2025, which the authors call 'really quite small'.

D2: firm surveys: 'the vast majority of firms (roughly 95 percent) report that AI had no net impact on their employment'; Census AI use 'now at about 9 percent' of businesses, 'About 27 percent' in the information sector.
sample_and_method: A: observational. Re-cuts of the authors' own ADP payroll data (the note gives no n), split by Zens et al. (2020) occupational interest-rate sensitivity, plus the event-study regression with firm-time fixed effects for ages 22 to 25. Data through October 2025. B: observational with quasi-experimental elements. Two representative surveys run with Statistics Denmark (late 2023 and late 2024), about 25,000 valid responses per round from 115,000 invited, about 7,000 workplaces, 11 exposed occupations (accountants, customer support specialists, financial advisors, HR professionals, IT support specialists, journalists, legal professionals, marketing professionals, office clerks, software developers, teachers), linked to monthly administrative records on earnings, hours and occupation. Difference-in-differences comparing adopters with non-adopters, and workplaces that encourage chatbot use with those that do not. B1 follows outcomes to June 2024; B2 to December 2024. Early-career defined as ages 22 to 25, following Canaries. C1: observational. Monthly CPS, November 2022 to July 2025, Duncan and Duncan dissimilarity index with a 12-month moving average, compared with 1984-1989, 1996-2002 and 2016-2019; OpenAI (Eloundou et al.) exposure scores and Anthropic Claude usage data. C2: observational. CPS occupation-level employment shares, median real hourly wages and unemployment rates; synthetic difference-in-differences with top-tercile exposure as treated and bottom tercile as donor pool, 2020 omitted, through Q1 2026. D1: observational. Lightcast job postings, 238 million US postings, September 2019 to August 2025, 767 six-digit SOC occupations, Eloundou et al. GPT-4 beta exposure quintiles, plotted against the federal funds rate; descriptive charts, no regression reported. D2: observational. CPS (via IPUMS) by quintile of AI exposure under five measures from four papers (Felten et al. as primary), plus Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey figures; descriptive charts.
evidence_offered: A: one scatter plot (interest-rate sensitivity against AI exposure, negatively correlated), two split-sample employment charts, and one event-study figure. No new tables or coefficients are given in the note. B: administrative register data linked to surveys, with stated confidence bounds, a replication of the Canaries age-group charts for Denmark (Appendix D.2), and workers' direct answers on whether chatbots changed their earnings. This is the only source here that observes actual adoption at the worker and workplace level. C: public CPS microdata with code and data published; C2 adds an explicit comparison-group design and confidence intervals. D1: timing of postings data relative to ChatGPT's release and Fed rate rises, a sector-composition statistic, a mechanical cohort-ageing argument, and enterprise-AI availability dates (OpenAI API 1 March 2023, ChatGPT Enterprise 28 August 2023). The argument is by coincidence of timing and plausibility, not by a test that separates the two explanations. D2: visual comparison of trend lines across exposure quintiles, repeated for five exposure measures.
data_vintage: A: published 9 February 2026; refers to the Canaries paper as 'last revised on November 13, 2025'; data through October 2025. It predates the authors' 12 August 2026 update, which was not examined for this item. B1: dated 9 May 2025, outcomes to June 2024, self-reported earnings effects as of November 2024. B2: NBER revision March 2026, outcomes to December 2024, survey fieldwork late 2024. B3: 6 October 2026, no new data. C1: published 1 October 2025, CPS through July 2025, Anthropic usage data from August/September 2025 releases. C2: published 7 May 2026, data through Q1 2026. Budget Lab tracker page dated 16 July 2026. D1: January 2026; written against the 26 August 2025 Canaries version but cites the 16% figure from the November 2025 revision; Lightcast data to August 2025. D2: published 10 August 2025, before the Canaries paper (26 August 2025), so it is not a response to it; CPS through early 2025.
figure_provenance: Humlum and Vestergaard bound: two versions circulate under the same NBER number. May 2025 abstract: 'ruling out effects larger than 1%' at about one and a half years (data to June 2024). March 2026 abstract: 'ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after the launch of ChatGPT' (data to December 2024). The body of the May 2025 version already distinguished a 1% pooled bound from a 2% dynamic bound. Cite the version used; the 1% figure is no longer in the current abstract.

Humlum and Vestergaard title: the paper most people cite as 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects' is now titled 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI'. NBER states 'This paper was previously circulated under the title'. The framing shifted from 'small effects' to 'reorganisation before earnings move'.
Humlum and Vestergaard time savings: 2.8% in the body, 'average time savings of 3%' in the May 2025 abstract. Self-reported.

Canaries 13% versus 16%: per the authors' own note, 13% is 'our paper with data only through July' (2025) and 'about 16%' is 'by October 2025', both from the firm-time fixed-effect specification. D1 quotes 16% while stating its comments were written about the 26 August 2025 (13%) version. Later vintages (15%, 19%) are outside the sources opened here.

'33 months' (Budget Lab): November 2022 to July 2025 CPS, original source C1. Press coverage often presents this as 'no AI job loss'; the report's own claim is narrower: no discernible economy-wide disruption in occupational mix.

'0.30 versus 0.94 percentage points' (EIG): original source D2, unemployment-rate change 2022 to early 2025 for the most and least exposed quintiles under the Felten et al. AIOE measure. Under two LLM-based measures the same report finds the exposed group slightly worse off (0.2 and 0.3 points).

'Almost a half of the decline by June 2023' (D1): the Google authors' reading of the Canaries charts for software engineers and customer service workers; not a figure stated by the Stanford authors in the note opened here.
A web-search summary attributed to a third paper a claim that Canaries found a fall of 'around 6%' for the most exposed quintile. This was not traced to a primary source and should not be used.
population_and_transfer: None of these studies is about how people learn; all are labour-market studies of employed adults. A: US private-sector employees on ADP payrolls, ages 22 to 25, including software developers by name. Direct relevance to junior engineers. B: Danish employees in 11 exposed occupations including software developers; transfer to US or UK engineering teams depends on accepting the authors' argument that Denmark's labour market is flexible with similar adoption rates. It measures chatbot use to late 2024, before coding agents were common. C: the whole US workforce, with a small sub-sample of graduates aged 20 to 24; the authors say the data are too thin for the early-career group, so transfer to junior engineers is weak. D1: US job postings by occupation and seniority, including software engineers; about vacancies, not people. D2: US workers by exposure quintile, with a young-worker and recent-graduate cut.
outcome_measured: A: employment (payroll headcount) relative change. B: earnings, recorded hours, wages, occupation switching, workplace total employment, early-career employment share, job creation and destruction; plus self-reported time savings and new tasks. C1: occupational mix (dissimilarity index), employment share by exposure, exposure among the unemployed. C2: employment share, real hourly wages, unemployment rate. D1: job postings by exposure quintile and seniority. D2: unemployment rate, labour-force exit, occupation switching, industry employment. None measures skill, comprehension, retention or on-the-job performance.
limitations_stated: A: 'we can't be sure of the causality from this sort of analysis'; 'the available interest rate data do not have as much occupational granularity as the AI exposure data'; 'the Zens et al. (2020) estimates do not condition on age, and young workers may potentially have different occupational interest rate exposure than the workforce as a whole'; 'Since we don't have an experiment where we can compare a world with AI to one without, this will remain an active area'.

B2: occupation-level 'Confidence bands are again wide for these occupation-specific estimates and should therefore be interpreted with caution'; the paper frames nulls as early ('the absence of measurable labor market effects is not evidence that nothing is happening'); time savings are self-reported; B1 notes 'We do not have sufficient statistical power to detect comparable pass-through effects in our difference-in-differences' design and asks that pass-through rates be read 'with some caution'. Survey respondents are, by construction, employed in the occupation at survey time.

C1: 'our analysis is not predictive of the future'; results on recent graduates 'should be interpreted with caution particularly given small sample sizes'; OpenAI exposure 'is not based on actual usage'; 'data from Claude usage alone is not representative'; 'Better data is needed'.

C2: exposure metrics 'are ultimately informed guesses'; averaging across an exposed group 'could actually hide effects'; the design cannot separate AI from 'other events, like the rise in remote work, that are closely correlated with exposure to AI'; CPS is 'somewhat underpowered for subgroup analysis, like the 22–27 year old recent college graduates'; 'LLMs are constantly improving, such that the economic impacts from early models seem likely to be smaller than those of recent models'.

D1: 'absence of evidence is not the same as evidence of absence'; 'We are still in the early innings of the AI transformation'; 'many of the key intellectual questions here are still to be settled conclusively'. The essay states no limitations of its own postings data or of the interest-rate argument.

D2: 'The lack of causal evidence is a problem ... for all of our analyses presented here'; the exposure measure 'is agnostic as to whether AI is a complement or substitute to workers'; new entrants 'are a small portion of the labor force' and 'may not show up in this industry-level analysis'.
counter_evidence: Against the null findings: the Stanford note reports the fixed-effects decline for exposed 22 to 25 year olds is 'growing' and has 'not shown a reversal' as of October 2025, i.e. it survives controls for firm-wide shocks, which a pure interest-rate story acting at firm level would not predict.

Against D1's interest-rate mechanism: the Stanford note finds AI exposure and interest-rate sensitivity negatively correlated using the same Zens et al. (2020) source D1 cites, and the Budget Lab (C2) finds, on pre-pandemic data, that AI-exposed occupations are 'generally less sensitive to the business cycle than unexposed occupations'. C2 adds that this did not hold in the post-2022 period.

Against the Canaries AI reading: Humlum and Vestergaard find the same early-career fall in Denmark but no difference between adopting and non-adopting workplaces; D1 shows postings in exposed occupations peaked in spring 2022; B3 cites Frank et al. (2026, 'AI-Exposed Jobs Deteriorated before ChatGPT') and Lambert and Schindler (2026, remote work) for pre-existing trends. Those two papers were not opened.

Against using Humlum and Vestergaard as a rebuttal of Canaries: their own text allows 'anticipatory hiring freezes unrelated to actual adoption' as a driver. A firm that stops hiring juniors because it expects AI to do the work, without yet encouraging chatbot use, would show up as a null in their design. Their data also end in December 2024, the year the Stanford authors say the controlled effect begins.

Against D2 as a rebuttal: it predates Canaries, uses unemployment rather than employment counts, and on the two LLM-based exposure measures it does find slightly higher relative unemployment for exposed workers.
alternative_explanations: Monetary tightening from March 2022 hitting rate-sensitive sectors where AI-exposed jobs cluster (D1). Disputed by the Stanford note.

Mechanical cohort ageing: any broad hiring freeze shrinks a narrow 22 to 25 band faster than older bands, with no layoffs and no targeting of juniors (D1). This is an argument about the measure, and it applies to any cause of reduced hiring, including AI.
Pre-existing decline: postings in exposed occupations peaked March to April 2022 and occupational-mix shifts were 'well on their way during 2021' (D1, C1).
Post-pandemic over-hiring and correction in tech and information sectors (raised in D2 for publishing and data processing).
Remote work, which is correlated with AI exposure (C2 citing Kolko 2026; B3 citing Lambert and Schindler 2026).
Young workers always bear downturns: the job ladder is procyclical, more so for the young (D1 citing Haltiwanger, Hyatt and McEntarfer 2018).

Anticipation: firms freezing junior hiring in expectation of AI, ahead of real adoption (Humlum and Vestergaard, section 3.4). This would still be an AI effect on entry-level hiring, but one based on belief, not on demonstrated substitution.
Offsetting effects inside the 'exposed' group: some exposed occupations expand and some contract, averaging to zero (C2).

relevance_to_essay: This item bounds the first of the essay's two findings. The safe statement is that employment of 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed jobs, software developers included, has fallen in US payroll data and in Danish register data, and that economists disagree on how much of that is AI. The Stanford authors call their own result suggestive and not causal, and now place the part that survives firm-level controls in 2024 and after. An essay that says 'AI is why juniors are not being hired' overstates the evidence. An essay that says 'fewer juniors are being hired into these roles, whatever the mix of causes' is supported, and the leadership question (who will be senior in five years) does not depend on settling the cause. It has no bearing on whether learning with AI weakens comprehension.
implications_for_training_design: None directly: no source here tests any training format, frequency or feedback method. Three indirect points. First, Humlum and Vestergaard find employer initiatives matter: in the May 2025 version, 30% of employees had received training, and encouragement nearly doubled take-up (47% to 83%); the revised paper reports that use and reported benefits peak where encouragement is combined with enterprise tools and training. That is evidence that organised employer effort changes how AI is used, not that it improves skill. Second, they find AI is absorbed through task reorganisation (new tasks in content generation, AI oversight and AI integration) before pay or hours move, which suggests what juniors need to learn is shifting toward review and oversight. Third, the Google/EIG essay itself says on-the-job training will need rethinking 'especially should AI take over tasks which were previously seen as formative', which is the essay's premise stated by authors otherwise sceptical of the displacement story.
open_questions: How much of the early-career decline is AI, interest rates, remote work or post-pandemic correction. No source separates them, and the Stanford authors say no experiment exists.
Whether firms are cutting junior hiring in anticipation of AI without having adopted it, which the Danish design cannot detect.
Whether the Danish null still holds after December 2024, once coding agents became widespread.
Whether the Canaries decline is specific to software developers once firm-time effects are included; the note gives no developer-specific number.
What the Stanford authors' August 2026 update does to the timing and interest-rate arguments made in the February 2026 note [uncertain: not examined here].
Whether the Budget Lab's later 2026 tracker updates changed its 'no clear footprint' reading [uncertain: only the 16 July 2026 takeaways were read].
